segments.title: Why the Soviet threat made defence spending easier to justify
segments.body: The Soviet Union dominated Cold War defence planning. Preparing to meet the Soviet threat came to stand in for judging what risks a country faced. A government could point to an adversary when it asked for money. A navy with interests to protect and no obvious opponent had a harder case to make.

evidence.note: Cold War planners came to treat managing the Soviet threat as equivalent to managing risk.
A government can point to a particular opponent when making the case for defence funds.

segments.summary: During the Cold War, a government seeking defence funds could identify the Soviet Union as the opponent it expected to face.

segments.title: Piracy and the case for keeping ships on station
segments.body: A country that relies on global sea trade is exposed to disruption every day. Piracy can flare up suddenly, and an immediate response requires ships in position when it happens. While shipping moves freely, it is easy to assume the trouble will never come. The country's reliance on those routes continues either way.

evidence.note: An immediate response to piracy depends on having ships stationed where trade is at risk.
People can acknowledge a standing risk and still dismiss the prospect that anything will happen.

segments.summary: The time to decide where ships are needed is while the trade routes are quiet. If piracy breaks out, distance matters immediately.

segments.title: An unlocked door and Great-Aunt Bertha's surprise visit
segments.body: Suppose a door on an isolated house has no working lock. Hardly anyone passes, so the householder sees little reason to fix it. Great-Aunt Bertha usually lives on the other side of the world, but she could still turn up with plans to bake her dreadful plum biscuits. A working lock would let the householder decide whether to let her in, without having to predict the visit.

evidence.note: The householder considers whether the doors and windows even have locks, then dismisses a door that will not lock because so few people pass.
Bertha usually lives on the other side of the world. If she made a surprise visit, an unlocked door would let her walk in.

segments.summary: A householder who rarely sees anyone pass has good reason to expect a quiet day. An unexpected visitor can still walk straight in.

segments.title: Why cyber threats can be nearly continuous
segments.body: An identifiable threat usually grows and recedes. Cybersecurity can follow a different pattern because almost anyone can pose a threat. One person acting alone is a possible source, as is a nation state. Even as the source changes, there may be little let-up in the threat itself.

evidence.note: Individuals and states can both pose cyber threats, keeping risk management necessary almost all the time.

segments.summary: In cybersecurity, a threat can come from so many different sources that managing the risk is an almost continuous job.

segments.title: Can two ships keep one escort available?
segments.body: One explanation for cuts to the Royal Navy's escorts is confidence that future demand can be forecast far enough ahead. Suppose two ships share a role and planners count on one always being available. Sending one to sea at short notice can mean delaying its maintenance. The same problem arises ashore if planners allow for one dry dock and more ships need it than expected. The promise of continuous cover depends on being able to predict the demands of defence, national security and foreign policy over the long term.

evidence.note: The case for assigning two units to a role assumes that demand will stay within the forecast.
An unexpected deployment can delay maintenance. Demand for a single dry dock can also exceed the forecast.

segments.summary: An urgent deployment can put off a ship's maintenance, and a single dry dock can face more work than planners expected.

segments.title: NATO's missing adversary and the 'end of history'
segments.body: One reading of the 'end of history' is that it marked a real easing of the threat to NATO and the Western powers. Their most obvious adversary, the Soviet Union, had disappeared. What passed for risk analysis still centred on the Cold War question of who threatened the West. With no obvious successor to the Soviet Union, it was easy to expect lasting peace. That way of judging security said little about the risks that remained.

evidence.note: The 'end of history' marked a lessening of the threat in this interpretation. NATO had lost its most obvious adversary.
Western confidence in peace rested on a threat assessment that still passed for risk analysis.

segments.summary: When the Soviet Union disappeared, the absence of an obvious adversary told NATO little about whether its other risks had changed.
